title: A fence around the Torah
hookLine: rabbis add protective rules around Torah laws

lines: THE RAILING GOES IN FEET BACK.
cards: At the top of a cliff there's a beautiful view, and a sheer drop. Nobody puts the warning at the very edge; by the time you're reading it there, one bad step is all it takes. So the railing goes in a few feet back.
You can still see everything. You just can't stumble over. It isn't the cliff.
It's what keeps you from the cliff. The opening teaching of Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, asks the sages to build one of these.

teach.h: MAKE A FENCE AROUND THE TORAH.
teach.b: Seyag. It's the Hebrew word for a fence, and in Jewish law it names a protective rule the sages add around a Torah law to keep people from breaking it.

First, the source, which you met long ago: the first mishnah of Avot tells the sages to be careful in judgment, to raise up many students, and to make a fence around the Torah. Second, what one looks like.
On the Sabbath, as the sages read the Torah, a person may not carry things out from a house into the street.
The Mishnah in tractate Shabbat adds a rule for Friday: a tailor shouldn't go out with his needle close to dark, in case he forgets it's there and carries it once the Sabbath begins.
The fence sits a little way back from the edge. Third, fences can go too far, and the tradition says so itself. In the garden, God told Adam not to eat from the tree.
But when Eve repeats the command, she adds something: "neither shall ye touch it." A teaching in Avot de-Rabbi Natan imagines Adam built that fence, and the serpent used it.
It pushed her against the tree: you touched it and nothing happened, so eating won't hurt either.
The lesson the sages draw: don't make the fence more important than what it guards, or when the fence falls, the garden goes with it. Fourth, fences aren't only legal.
Rabbi Akiva, also in Avot, names others: tradition is a fence for the Torah, and silence is a fence for wisdom.

how: Rabbinic rules often work as fences: for example, the sages added Sabbath rules that keep people well back from the work the Torah forbids, and Jews who keep them treat the fences as part of the law.

o: a Torah law that can never be changed
a boundary marking where a town ends
a protective rule set around a Torah law

p: make a fence around the Torah
not carried out close to dark on Friday

s: a fence is the same as the Torah law it protects
it's a protective rule set back from the edge, like a railing before a cliff.
the tradition itself warns that a fence can backfire
Avot de-Rabbi Natan reads Eve's 'neither shall ye touch it' as a fence the serpent used.
fences in Avot are only legal rules
Rabbi Akiva calls silence a fence for wisdom.

games.q: carrying from house to street is forbidden on the Sabbath. you're a sage worried a tailor will forget the needle tucked in his clothes. what do you do?
o: leave the law as it is.
tell him not to go out with his needle close to dark on Friday.
games.why: the Mishnah in tractate Shabbat sets that fence: no going out with the needle close to dark, in case he forgets and carries it once the Sabbath begins.

practice: Pick one thing you want to protect, like sleep, a morning walk or an hour without a screen, and find the cliff edge, the moment it usually slips away.
Then step back from it: what small rule, set earlier, would keep you from the edge, like the phone out of the bedroom? Keep it small, and remember which is the fence and which is the garden.

wordCard.voice: Seyag. A fence: a protective rule the sages set around a Torah law, so people stay far from breaking it. Today's word.
